l2_section.x: Said bin Sultan and the making of Zanzibar, 1800 to 1845

Salim's chapter in UNESCO's volume VI starts from a coast that was not Omani. Around 1800 Oman's presence was clear only at Mombasa, Zanzibar and Kilwa, and even in Mombasa the Mazrui family acted almost independently of Muscat with the help of Swahili shaykhs of the 'Twelve Nations', a federation of the Three Nations and the Nine Nations. Elsewhere jumbes and diwanis ruled with their own regalia and a mix of customary and Islamic law. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Said bin Sultan, imam from 1806, saw himself as a merchant prince first. Oman had grown rich by carrying goods under a neutral flag during the Napoleonic Wars, and by 1802 its agents on the coast were sending 40000 Maria Theresa dollars a year to Muscat. Said signed a commercial treaty with Ile de France (now Mauritius) in 1807 and used the Swahili towns' own quarrels to advance. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

His advance was slow and depended on local politics. A Pate and Mazrui force was beaten at Shela on Lamu in 1812 to 1813, which led Lamu to ask for his protection. He took Pemba in 1823, and a British naval officer, Captain Owen, declared a protectorate over Mombasa in 1824 that ended in 1826. Busa'idi attacks on Fort Jesus failed in 1828, 1829 and 1833 because the Swahili Three and Nine Nations backed the Mazrui. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Mombasa fell only in 1837, after the able Mazrui ruler Salim bin Ahmed died in 1835 and his successor lost the shaykhs' support. Even then Said's governor shared administration with the shaykhs. Salim's point is that Omani rule was a bargain with local powers more than a conquest. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Zanzibar then outgrew its rivals. Said moved his capital there after 1837, and it became the main market on the coast for ivory, slaves, cloves and gum copal and the main importer of cottons, beads, guns and gunpowder. He signed commercial treaties with Britain in 1839 and France in 1844, and with the United States, whose cloth 'Merekani' became a household word. American sales there rose from 100000 dollars in 1838 to 550000 at his death in 1856, which is 5.5 times (our arithmetic). {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Salim gives two dates for the American treaty in the same chapter, 1837 in one place and 1833 in another. Check the treaty's date in a second source before you repeat it. His chapter also dates the final Portuguese expulsion south of the Rovuma to 1728, while this lesson, following volume V, gives 1729. {{gha6-salim}} {{gha5-coast}}

Cloves made the new economy. Said used slave labour on about forty-five plantations and by 1840 produced two-thirds of the 8000 frasilas exported from Zanzibar, which is about 5300 frasilas (our arithmetic). A frasila was about 35 pounds. Bombay's imports of Zanzibari cloves rose from 29000 dollars in 1837 to 1838 to 97000 five years later, about 3.3 times (our arithmetic). Omani families took land in northern and western Zanzibar, and the Hadimu were left with the south and east. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Asian merchants and financiers were central. The Zanzibar customs were farmed out to an Asian merchant by 1804, and Jairam Sewji held the farm from 1834 to 1853. The sultans stayed in debt to the customs farmers, and Asian capital supplied Arab and Swahili caravans. Salim stresses that this gave the Asian merchants a strong economic place without political power. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

The figures for the trade in people are disputed. Nicholls gave 20000 a year, while Sheriff put the 1830s figure at only 2500 a year, which is eight times lower (our arithmetic), and Alpers challenges both, finding Sheriff too low. In the 1850s some 60000 of Zanzibar's 150000 people were slaves, which is 40 per cent (our arithmetic). The Hamerton Treaty of 1847, which banned exports beyond Said's East African dominions, proved 'decidedly inadequate'. {{gha6-salim}} [CONTESTED]

Said's household shows the mixing. Most of his wives were African, his children spoke Kiswahili rather than Arabic, and every later sultan of the century was born of a slave woman. Salim also contrasts a 'raw' Omani or Yemeni Arab, called a Mmanga or a Mshihiri respectively, with a settled, Africanised counterpart in the Swahili towns. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Salim's wider reading is that Zanzibar's merchant capitalism tied East Africa to a Western system and led to 'underdevelopment', through unequal exchange and cheap consumer imports that hurt Lamu's and the Benadir ports' textile industries. This is an argument of the same kind as Wallerstein's in Module 8. Weigh it against the evidence of growth in cloves and trade. {{gha6-salim}} [CONTESTED]

l2_section.title: Worked example: how large was the disagreement over slave numbers (our arithmetic)
steps: Nicholls gives 20000 slaves a year and Sheriff 2500 a year for the 1830s.
20000 divided by 2500 is 8, so the higher estimate is eight times the lower.
Over a decade the two figures imply 200000 against 25000 people, a difference of 175000. A gap that large means a single figure should never be quoted without its author.

l2_checks.q: A website says Sayyid Said conquered the whole East African coast in one campaign and ruled it from Muscat. What does Salim's chapter suggest is wrong with that account?
o: He took Mombasa in 1837 after failed attacks
The ruler, because Britain held the coast under a protectorate from 1824 to 1856
The place, because he never ruled any coastal town, only a Persian fleet
The date, because the Mazrui held Mombasa until the British conquest of 1895
Nothing, because he captured Mombasa, Pate and Lamu in a single year
l2_checks.w: He needed four attempts at Fort Jesus, depended on splits among the Mazrui and the shaykhs, and left much local autonomy, so conquest alone is the wrong word. {{gha6-salim}}

l2_checks.q: A documentary says 'exactly 20000 people a year were carried from the East African coast in the 1830s'. How should a careful viewer treat the figure?
o: Trust it, because Alpers confirmed it and Sheriff's lower figure was withdrawn
Trust it, because it was set down by Said's own customs officers in Zanzibar
Treat it as one contested estimate of several
Average it with Sheriff's 2500 to reach a stable figure of 11250 a year
Reject it, because every nineteenth-century figure is false and none can be used
l2_checks.w: Salim reports Nicholls at 20000, Sheriff at 2500 and Alpers disputing both, so the number is a contested estimate. {{gha6-salim}}

l3_section.x: Salim's chapter qualifies the line that the interior joined long-distance trade only about 1800. Foreign goods reached inland Tanzania in the eighteenth century through regional exchange, and the Giriama had supplied ivory to the coast earlier still. His main point is that African traders began the caravans, and Arab and Swahili caravans followed later. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

In the south Yao and Bisa traders carried ivory and slaves from the Lake Nyasa region to Kilwa Kivinje, a mainland village 27 kilometres from the old island town, which had an Omani governor by 1819 and by 1850 was the most important town between Mozambique and Zanzibar. In the north the Nyamwezi and Sumbwa reached the coast around 1800 through Ugogo, and the Kamba and Giriama traded ivory with the Swahili. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

The dates of the first long caravans are short and exact. The first non-African caravan reached Unyamwezi in 1824, Lief bin Said, who was half Arab and half Nyamwezi, marched to Lake Tanganyika in 1831 and sent his own caravan in 1837, an Arab caravan crossed the lake to Kazembe in 1841, and by 1845 coastal traders had reached Buganda. Ivory prices rose, doubling at Surat in India between 1804 and 1808. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Africans led the caravans in the north. By the 1820s the Kamba were fitting out their own caravans, and Kivui Mwenda's caravans had about 300 men. Kamba caravans dominated the northern route in the 1830s to 1850s until bigger and better-armed Arab and Swahili caravans pushed inland from the late 1850s. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Trade changed social life. After 1830 many Digo, Giriama, Rabai and Duruma left their fortified kaya villages for trade and pasture, which weakened the elders and the age-sets and raised rich individuals such as the Giriama Ngonyo and the Digo Mwakikonge. Peoples also married and made blood-brotherhoods across lines, and healing and divining practices spread. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Coastal culture travelled with the caravans. The kanzu was worn as far inland as Buganda, the Yao chief Mataka rebuilt his capital in coastal style, and Rumanyika of Karagwe furnished his palace with mirrors and clocks. Islam won rulers first and spread into rural areas, and Burton found Kiswahili widely spoken by the 1850s, so that the language travelled further than the faith. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

Not every people took part. The Kikuyu never traded with the coast and later showed no interest in the caravans, and Maasai disorder kept coastal traders out for years. In 1837 the Wa-Kwavi mauled an Arab-Swahili party outside Mombasa. Salim adds that the Tanganyika hinterland was more affected by the coast than the Kenyan one in this period. {{gha6-salim}} [PROBABLE]

l3_section.title: Worked example: how quickly did the caravans spread (our arithmetic)
steps: The first non-African caravan reached Unyamwezi in 1824, an Arab caravan reached Kazembe in 1841 and coastal traders reached Buganda by 1845.
From 1824 to 1841 is 17 years, and from 1824 to 1845 is 21 years.
Within about two decades of the first non-African caravan inland, traders had reached the farthest kingdoms of East and Central Africa, using routes African traders had already opened.

l3_checks.q: A textbook says Arab traders opened up the East African interior in the 1800s and brought long-distance trade to peoples who had none. What does Salim's chapter suggest is wrong with that sentence?
o: The century, because he says the interior was already trading with the coast in 1500
Nothing, because he says the first inland caravans were Arab-led from 1800
The effect, because he says the caravans did not change inland societies at all
The place, because he says no trade reached Tanzania until the 1860s
African traders began the caravans first
l3_checks.w: He says the caravan trade was initiated by Africans such as the Yao, Nyamwezi, Kamba and Giriama, and that Arab and Swahili caravans moved inland later, especially from the late 1850s. {{gha6-salim}}
